Risk Is Not Destiny: Unmasked Penetrance of Parkinson Disease in Gaucher Disease. 106 10 5 5 2026 e218074 e218074 Neurology 42085647 Background and Objectives Glucocerebrosidase ( GBA1 ) pathogenic variants are strongly associated with Parkinson disease (PD); however, insufficient data exist on the prevalence of PD among patients with Gaucher disease type 1 (GD1) (biallelic pathogenic GBA1 variants). Also, penetrance estimates in patients with GD are lower than expected given their severely diminished enzymatic activity. We aimed to estimate the age-specific risk of PD in patients with GD1, overall and by GBA1 genotype. Methods Participants were patients with GD1 in the International Collaborative Gaucher Group Gaucher Registry, a global GD database, as of February 2024. We longitudinally collected data on clinical diagnosis of PD and dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) and report of motor (rest tremor, falls) and nonmotor (cognitive impairment, REM sleep behavior disorder, loss of sense of smell, autonomic dysfunction) signs/symptoms. In addition to a conservative physician-based PD and DLB diagnosis, we created a liberal definition of possible parkinsonian syndrome (pPS; ≥2 signs/symptoms, PD, or DLB) to test whether previous low penetrance estimates stem from underdiagnosis. Patients were classified as pPS at earliest of the following dates: PD diagnosis, DLB diagnosis, or report of second sign/symptom. We separately estimated age-specific prevalence of PD and pPS using Kaplan-Meier survival curves. Results Among 1,618 patients with GD1 (median age at last follow-up 47.8 years; 53% female), 51 were diagnosed with PD and 86 as pPS. The age-specific prevalence (95% CI) of PD and pPS was 4.0% (2.7–5.7) and 6.0% (4.5–7.9) at 60 years and 12.2% (8.6–17.0) and 22.9% (17.1–30.1) at 80 years, respectively. Patients with 2 mild pathogenic GBA1 variants had a qualitatively lower prevalence of PD and pPS vs patients with one mild variant. Discussion In this large cohort of 1,618 patients, approximately one-in-nine patients with GD1 were diagnosed with PD and more than one-in-five patients were diagnosed with PD/DLB or experienced movement disorder symptoms by 80 years. Most patients were from North America and Europe; generalizability to other regions is unknown. Our finding that most patients remain free of PD despite very low residual enzyme activity informs the hypothesis that acid ß-glucosidase levels directly predict risk of PD. pmc-status-qastatus 0 pmc-status-live yes pmc-status-embargo no pmc-status-released yes pmc-prop-open-access yes pmc-prop-olf no pmc-prop-manuscript no pmc-prop-legally-suppressed no pmc-prop-has-pdf yes pmc-prop-has-supplement no pmc-prop-pdf-only no pmc-prop-suppress-copyright no pmc-prop-is-real-version no pmc-prop-is-scanned-article no pmc-prop-preprint no pmc-prop-in-epmc yes pmc-license-ref CC BY-NC-ND OPEN-ACCESS TRUE SPECIAL-PROPERTY EDITORIAL Introduction Variants in the gene glucocerebrosidase ( GBA1 ) encoding the lysosomal enzyme acid ß-glucosidase are strongly associated with Parkinson disease (PD). 1 Biallelic pathogenic variants result in Gaucher disease (GD), which is broadly organized into 3 types based on the presence of childhood neurodegenerative disease (Gaucher disease type 2 and Gaucher disease type 3) or the absence of early neurologic involvement (Gaucher disease type 1 [GD1]). Risk of PD is elevated both in patients with GD and, to a lesser degree, in GBA1 heterozygotes (i.e., carriers). 2 GBA1 pathogenic variants have also been linked to other forms of synucleinopathies, including dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB), rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorders (RBD), 3,4 and multiple system atrophy. 5 The mechanism linking GBA1 pathogenic variants, GD1 and PD, remains controversial. 6 The prevailing hypothesis is that loss of acid ß-glucosidase function leads to accumulation of lipid substrates, which may enhance the aggregation of alpha synuclein as happens in PD. 6-8 However, this hypothesis is not consistent with current penetrance estimations of PD in patients with GD1, 2,9 which are not appreciably different than penetrance estimations in GBA1 heterozygotes. 10-13 Effective therapies for GD have enabled patients with GD1 to survive to advanced ages, where they are at increased risk of certain age-related conditions including PD and multiple myeloma. 14,15 Although patients with GD report concern for developing PD, 16 existing data on age-specific risk (i.e., penetrance) necessary for counseling patients and guiding screening are limited. Among 427 US and Israeli patients with GD1, risk of PD was estimated as 4.7% at age 60 years and 9.1% at age 80 years. 2 Similar estimates were separately reported using earlier data from the same US 10 and Israeli sites. 17 In GD, there is wide phenotypic variability across the approximately 646 known, unique GBA1 pathogenic variants, 18 with p.N409S (previously known as p.N370S) homozygosity associated with greater retention of residual acid ß-glucosidase enzyme activity and GD1. GBA1 variants also appear to be associated with PD severity: in 2 large and geographically diverse studies of heterozygous GBA1 carriers, presence of a severe GBA1 pathogenic variant (vs a mild GBA1 variant) was associated with elevated risk of PD and earlier age at PD onset. 19,20 In GD, the frequency of pathogenic variants is highly variable across ethnicities and geographies 21 ; thus, large studies in diverse populations are needed to generate more precise estimates of age-specific PD risk across the full spectrum of disease. Such estimates are necessary for guiding the screening of motor and nonmotor signs/symptoms, patient counseling, identifying high-risk patients for potential neuroprotective therapies, and focusing efforts on biomarker discovery for early detection and treatment. More robust estimates may also inform understanding of risk of PD in patient populations outside of GD. The objective of this study was to estimate the age-specific risk of Parkinson disease in patients with GD1, overall and by category of GBA1 genotype. To refine penetrance estimates, we used longitudinal data from the International Collaborative Gaucher Group (ICGG) Gaucher Registry ( NCT00358943 , funded by Sanofi), an ongoing, multicenter, observational program collecting data on routine clinical outcomes of patients with GD from approximately 280 sites across 64 countries for over 30 years. 22 In previous studies of GD1, risk of PD was lower than expected, suggesting possible underestimation of PD. 2 To estimate an upper bound of risk, including patients with PD and other Parkinson-like conditions (e.g., DLB) and those who were symptomatic but may have not yet been formally diagnosed with PD or DLB (e.g., prodromal disease), we also estimated risk of possible parkinsonian syndrome (pPS), which we defined as the presence of PD, DLB, or 2 or more movement disorder signs/symptoms. Methods Study Population The ICGG Gaucher Registry enrolls patients with a confirmed diagnosis of GD, with the treating physician assigning the GD type. In the absence of biallelic pathogenic variants, individuals who were carriers of other GBA1 variants linked to PD (e.g., E365K or T408M) were not included, as these variants alone are not pathogenic for GD. Patients with GD1 who had information on PD and/or pPS status (see “Outcome definition”) as of February 2024 were included. Site personnel abstracted demographic data from medical records using the following categories (multiple categories could be selected): for race, American Indian or Alaska Native, Asian, Black, Native Hawaiian or other Pacific Islander, White, not reported, unknown; for ethnicity, Hispanic or Latino, not Hispanic or Latino, not reported, unknown. Outcome Definition Because of the voluntary nature of the Registry, there is not a prespecified assessment schedule. Rather, the sites obtain data from medical records documenting regular care by the treating physician. Sites were instructed to abstract data on PD, other Parkinson-like conditions (e.g., DLB), and individual signs/symptoms from medical records using standardized case report forms (CRFs). Data were collected on whether the patient was diagnosed with PD or other Parkinson-like conditions, and, if so, their first date of diagnosis. If another Parkinson-like condition was selected, the specific type of condition (i.e., multiple system atrophy, progressive supranuclear palsy, vascular parkinsonism, Lewy body dementia, or other) was also queried. Similarly, sites abstracted medical record data were also on the presence of the following movement disorder signs/symptoms: motor symptoms (e.g., tremor, bradykinesia, rigidity), falls, cognitive impairment, RBD, loss of sense of smell, and autonomic dysfunction (e.g., loss of bladder control, fainting, erectile dysfunction) and the date on which each sign/symptom was first noted. For all data points collected in the Registry, including movement disorders, completion guidelines and training instructed the sites to enter data for all patients regardless of their outcome status. We defined 2 outcomes: (1) the conservative outcome of clinical diagnosis of PD and (2) the broader outcome of pPS ( Figure 1 ). For clinical diagnosis of PD, we defined time at event as the first date of PD diagnosis. For pPS, we included patients diagnosed with PD and those diagnosed with another Parkinson-like condition, or reporting 2 or more of the following symptoms: motor symptoms, falls, cognitive impairment, RBD, loss of sense of smell, and autonomic dysfunction. For pPS, time at event was defined as the date of first diagnosis of PD or another Parkinson-like condition (e.g., DLB) or the time at which at least 2 of the above signs/symptoms were reported, whichever came first. For the primary approach, we excluded patients who reported the outcome but were missing the outcome date (for PD, N = 3 and for pPS, N = 5). Patients who were never assessed for PD were excluded from PD analyses, and patients who were never assessed for PD, another Parkinson-like condition, or movement disorder signs/symptoms were excluded from pPS analyses. We categorized patients as having a “mild pathogenic GBA1 variant” if they had ≥1 p.N409S or p.R535H (previously known as p.R496H) variant. 23 Statistical Analysis Demographic and clinical characteristics were described overall, by PD and pPS status, and by age at PD diagnosis (<60 years or ≥60 years). Categorical variables were summarized using frequencies and percentages (n, %), and continuous variables were summarized using summary statistics (n, mean, standard deviation, median, 25th and 75th percentiles, minimum, and maximum). First, Kaplan-Meier survival curves in the overall population were used to estimate a) survival free of PD and b) survival free of pPS. We used a time scale of age in years, with follow-up beginning at birth and ending at time of event or last follow-up in the Registry. Next, we repeated these analyses for patients with 1 vs 2 mild pathogenic GBA1 variants in the subset of patients with ≥1 mild pathogenic GBA1 variant. Patients with no mild pathogenic GBA1 variants represent a heterogeneous group of high- and low-severity genotypes; therefore, we did not assess PD/pPS in this group. To facilitate the ability of health care providers to benchmark the risk in individual patients, age- and sex-specific proportions (95% confidence interval [CI]) of patients with PD and pPS were estimated at each 5-year increment between the ages of 60 and 80 years (inclusive). For the overall population (i.e., males and females combined), age-specific proportions were also presented by GBA1 category. Survival plots include Hall-Wellner confidence bands and are truncated at the time at which there were fewer than 5 patients at risk remaining. Second, Cox proportional hazards analyses were used to estimate hazard ratios (HRs) (95% CI) for PD or pPS in patients with 1 vs 2 mild pathogenic GBA1 variants after adjustment for disease severity. Models were restricted to the subset of patients with ≥1 mild pathogenic GBA1 variant who had data on ages at primary Gaucher treatment initiation and Gaucher diagnosis. A time scale of age in years was used, with follow-up beginning at birth and ending at time of event or last follow-up in the Registry. Although imiglucerase is not thought to cross the blood-brain barriers, neurologic stabilization or improvement has been documented in patients with GD3 receiving imiglucerase. 24 To account for any possible treatment effect, models were adjusted for sex and markers of severity, including GBA1 genotype category (1 vs 2 mild GBA1 pathogenic variants), time-varying treatment status, time-varying bone crisis status, and ages at primary Gaucher treatment initiation and Gaucher diagnosis. Sensitivity Analyses Bias may be introduced when comparing risk of PD between treated and untreated patients because treated patients must live long enough to be treated. For this reason, Cox proportional hazards analyses were repeated in the subset of the population who were ever treated and had information on date of primary Gaucher treatment initiation. For this analysis, we used a time scale of time since treatment in years, beginning at treatment initiation and ending at the time of event or last follow-up in the Registry; models were adjusted for time-varying bone crisis status, age at primary Gaucher treatment initiation, and GBA1 genotype category (1 vs 2 mild pathogenic variants). To assess the effect of excluding the small subgroup of patients missing date of PD or pPS diagnosis/classification, we summarized the demographic and clinical characteristics of these patients and conducted a sensitivity analysis including these patients in Kaplan-Meier calculations using imputed dates. To impute date of PD diagnosis, we first calculated the median time between PD diagnosis and most recent follow-up in the population of patients with information on date of PD diagnosis. We then imputed the date of PD diagnosis for the patients diagnosed with PD but missing the date of PD diagnosis by subtracting this value from their age at the most recent follow-up. The missing date of report of ≥2 signs/symptoms was imputed similarly. For descriptive analyses, we describe differences between groups as “qualitative” to differentiate them from analyses calculating statistical significance. SAS version 9.4 (SAS Institute Inc, Cary, NC) was used for all statistical analyses. Standard Protocol Approvals, Registrations, and Patient Consents The study population consisted of patients with GD enrolled in the ICGG Gaucher Registry ( NCT00358943 ), which is governed by an independent board of advisors who are experts in the care of patients with GD. The Registry is a voluntary program for tracking the natural history and outcomes of patients with GD regardless of their treatment status or the product with which they were treated. Patients were enrolled in the Registry by site investigators, and written informed consent was obtained from all patients per study site regulations and verified by study monitors. Institutional Review Boards' approval was obtained at each site. We adhered to STROBE guidelines for cohort studies. Data Availability Access to the anonymized data for this study will be available from the corresponding author upon reasonable requests from qualified researchers, contingent on approval by the author group. Results Among 7,208 patients in the Registry, 6,087 were diagnosed with GD1 and 1,618 of those patients had data on PD and pPS status. Among patients with available data, most patients were White (89.2%), followed by American Indian or Alaska Native (5.0%), Asian (2.6%), Black (1.7%), and Native Hawaiian or other Pacific Islander (0.3%); 1.2% of patients were multiple races. Most patients were of Ashkenazi Jewish descent (73.8%), followed by Arab (3.1%), Jewish—unspecified (2.9%), Sephardic Jewish (2.2%); 19.9% of patients were of another, unspecified ancestry. Patients from Europe, Middle East, Eurasia, and Africa (52.7%) and North America (45.3%) were heavily represented, but the study population also included patients from Latin America (1.2%) and Japan Pacific and Asia (0.8%). Approximately 90% patients had at least one mild pathogenic GBA1 variant ( Table 1 ). For this analysis, patients were followed from birth until the event of interest or last Registry follow-up, yielding a median (25th, 75th percentile) age of 47.8 years (32.2, 62.1). Total person-years across the entire study population was 75,474 for PD and 75,283 for pPS. Of the 1,618 patients included in the study population, 51 (3.2%) were diagnosed with PD, with a median age of 56.5 (47.8, 65.3) years (25th, 75th percentile) at diagnosis. Patients diagnosed with PD by age 60 years (n = 29) vs those diagnosed by the age of ≥60 years (n = 22) were qualitatively more likely to be male (55.2% vs 45.5%) and have a single mild pathogenic GBA1 variant (63.0% vs 45.5%) (eTable 1 ) . A total of 86 patients (5.3%) were classified as having pPS, with a median (25th, 75th percentile) age at classification of 57.5 (46.6, 68.1) years. The 86 patients with pPS comprised 51 patients diagnosed with PD described above (with or without DLB), 5 patients diagnosed with DLB, and 30 patients who reported 2 or more signs or symptoms but were never diagnosed with PD or DLB. Of the 51 patients diagnosed with PD, 10 reported ≥2 signs/symptoms before being diagnosed with PD and were, therefore, classified as pPS at the time that ≥2 signs/symptoms were reported. Twenty-one (70.0%) patients without PD or DLB reported 2 signs or symptoms, 8 (26.7%) reported 3 signs or symptoms, and one (3.3%) reported 5 signs or symptoms. The number of patients reporting each unique combination of signs/symptoms is reported in eTable 2. Among patients with pPS, the most prevalent individual signs/symptoms were motor symptoms (86.0%), falls (36.0%), autonomic dysfunction (30.2%), and cognitive impairment (27.9%) (data not shown). Among all patients reporting at least one sign or symptom (i.e., not limited to those meeting pPS criteria), the median (25th, 75th percentiles) age at onset of individual signs/symptoms is presented in Figure 2 . The onset of motor symptoms appeared earliest while diagnosis with DLB occurred later. However, these findings do not necessarily represent the progression of symptoms within an individual, as some patients reported only one sign/symptom. Kaplan-Meier curves for survival free of PD are presented for the overall population in Figure 3A and by GBA1 genotype categories in Figure 3B . Figure 4, A and B show overall and GBA1 genotype-specific survival free of pPS, respectively. In the overall population, the proportion of patients (95% CI) with PD and pPS was 4.0% (2.7–5.7) and 6.0% (4.5–7.9), respectively, at 60 years of age; 7.8% (5.7–10.6) and 11.8% (9.2–15.2), respectively, at 70 years; and 12.2% (8.6–17.0) and 22.9% (17.1–30.1), respectively, at 80 years ( Table 2 ). Among patients with at least one mild pathogenic GBA1 variant, risk of both PD and pPS was qualitatively lower in patients with 2 vs 1 mild pathogenic variant throughout follow-up. eTables 3 and 4 are extended versions of Table 2 that show the proportion of patients with PD and pPS, respectively, across 5-year age categories and by sex. Sex-specific estimates are not shown for GBA1 genotype categories because of small sample sizes. In Cox proportional hazards models in patients with at least one mild pathogenic GBA1 variant (N = 1,356), patients with 2 mild pathogenic GBA1 variants had a qualitatively lower risk (HR = 0.60; 95% CI 0.32–1.12) of PD compared with those with one mild pathogenic GBA1 variant (eTable 5). Similarly, patients with 2 mild pathogenic variants had a 53% (HR = 0.47; 95% CI 0.28–0.79) lower risk of pPS compared with those with one mild pathogenic variant (N = 1,356) (eTable 6). Women (vs men) had 16% and 10% lower risk of PD and pPS, respectively; however, no associations of sex, bone crisis, and treatment status with PD and pPS reached statistical significance (all p > 0.05). Sensitivity Analyses In Cox proportional hazards models restricted to treated patients with at least one mild pathogenic GBA1 variant (N = 1,135), patients with 2 mild pathogenic GBA1 variants had a qualitatively lower risk of PD (HR = 0.54; 95% CI 0.23–1.24) and a 57% lower risk of pPS (HR = 0.43; 95% CI 0.22–0.84) compared with those with one mild pathogenic GBA1 variant (eTables 7 and 8). eTables 9 and 10 show the age-specific proportion of patients with PD and pPS, respectively, using imputed dates for patients missing data on PD (N = 3)/pPS (N = 5) diagnosis/report. Estimates are similar to or slightly higher than those of the primary approach. Discussion In this analysis of 1,618 patients with GD1 from the ICGG Gaucher Registry, we present the most comprehensive assessment of age-specific PD risk in a GD1 population to date. To better capture the full spectrum of parkinsonian manifestations, including formally diagnosed PD, related syndromes, and prodromal cases, we introduced the term pPS to identify patients with significant movement disorder symptoms. By age 80 years, an estimated 12.2% of patients with GD1 had a confirmed PD diagnosis, whereas 22.9% exhibited parkinsonian features, with a qualitatively higher risk observed for those with 1 vs 2 mild GBA1 pathogenic variants. These findings have important implications for patient counseling, screening strategies, and early intervention, particularly for motor symptoms, which appeared earlier than other clinical features, and may allow for timely diagnosis and management. We assessed diagnosis of PD and DLB and reports of individual movement disorder signs/symptoms using standardized CRFs. This approach is a more refined assessment of PD compared with our previous Registry study in which we estimated age-specific risk of parkinsonism by querying free text responses on chronic disease for “Parkinson,” “Parkinsonism,” and related terms. 9 In our previous study, the estimated proportion of patients developing parkinsonism was 5%–7% by age 70 years and 9%–12% by age 80 years, 9 similar to findings for PD and lower than those for pPS in the current study. These findings are consistent with pPS being a relatively broader categorization than parkinsonism. Our findings align with previous studies in the US and Israel reporting age-specific risk of PD in patients with GD1 ( Table 3 ). By age 60 years, 4.0% of patients in this analysis of the ICGG Gaucher Registry were diagnosed with PD, compared with 1.0%–4.7% of patients in previous studies 2,10 ; by age 80 years, 12.2% of our study population was diagnosed with PD, compared with 9.1% in a previous study. 2 It is unknown whether PD sex ratios vary between idiopathic and GBA1-associated PD. Consistent with previous studies in patients with GD1 and GBA1 heterozygotes and idiopathic PD that have reported a higher prevalence of PD and DLB in men than women, 14,17,25,26 we report a (nonstatistically significant) 10.0%–16.0% decreased risk of PD and pPS in women. Our finding that most patients with GD1 remain free of PD or related signs/symptoms challenges the prevailing “loss of function” hypothesis, which posits a dose-response relationship between acid ß-glucosidase activity levels and risk of PD. This hypothesis is based on the premise that risk of PD is proportional to lower acid ß-glucosidase enzymatic activity and corresponding elevated substrate (glucosylceramide and glucosylsphingosine) levels. 7,8 This mechanism is supported by the fact that GBA1 variants that are associated with PD risk are indeed associated with loss of acid ß-glucosidase activity. In addition, among heterozygous GBA1 carriers, individuals with a severe GBA1 variant, who have relatively lower residual acid ß-glucosidase activity, 27 are at higher risk for PD than those with a mild GBA1 variant. 19,20 However, based on this hypothesis, we would have expected to see a notably higher PD penetrance in patients with GD1, which we have not observed here, even when taking a liberal approach to PD diagnosis using the pPS diagnosis. Although PD penetrance in patients with GD was somewhat higher than that previously reported in GBA1 heterozygotes ( Table 3 ), 2,10 we expected a more extreme difference given the meaningful difference in residual acid ß-glucosidase activity between these populations. Our findings suggest that reduced acid ß-glucosidase activity alone does not predict PD and other, yet unknown genetic and/or environmental factors modify PD penetrance. Results from Cox proportional hazards models adjusted for markers of severity were consistent with those from Kaplan-Meier survival curves. Cox proportional hazards models in treated patients showed no association between treatment status or age at treatment initiation and PD or pPS. However, these results should be interpreted with caution because it is possible that a true underlying association with treatment status/age at treatment initiation could not be detected because of the observational nature of the study. This could occur if part of the effect of treatment is accounted for by other variables in the model also related to severity (e.g., GBA1 genotype), which would diminish the magnitude of the observed association between treatment and PD. We defined “possible parkinsonian syndrome” to reflect the uncertainty inherent to an outcome that was defined using signs/symptoms that may have been self-reported, assessed without screening all patients, and be nonspecific or otherwise not confirmed as parkinsonism. However, 86% of patients classified with pPS were reported to have motor symptoms and 28% were reported to have cognitive impairment, suggesting that we have captured patients with significant risk for PD or alike synucleinopathy. This outcome allowed us to estimate an upper bound for PD, which may have been underdiagnosed in this and previous studies. Future studies should move toward greater diagnostic clarity through the systematic screening of all patients by movement disorder specialists. We considered several possible scenarios in which risk of PD or pPS may have been underestimated because of the omission of some patients with PD or pPS. First, we may have missed patients with PD who were not yet formally diagnosed; however, these patients would likely have been captured in our broader definition of pPS. Second, patients could have been missed if they had documented PD or 2 or more signs/symptoms, but this was not captured in the Registry. We minimized the potential for underreporting by instructing Registry staff to enter data for all patients, not just those with reported diagnoses or signs/symptoms. Third, we could have underestimated pPS if signs/symptoms were not documented in medical records. Finally, the age-specific risk of PD and pPS may have been underestimated because of the exclusion of patients with PD and/or pPS but missing the date of diagnosis/classification. Findings from a sensitivity analysis using imputed dates are similar or slightly higher than those of the primary approach, suggesting that such underestimation of PD/pPS risk is minimal. A major strength of our study was that PD, DLB, and patient-reported symptoms were ascertained from medical records by trained staff using standardized CRFs. However, we were limited in that it is unknown if patients underwent specific neurologic assessment to confirm the diagnosis of PD, PD-free status, or presence of signs/symptoms. We report similar point estimates as those from previous studies in which all patients were screened by movement disorder specialists, suggesting that the degree to which PD may have been over or underdiagnosed was minimal. 2 Full GBA1 sequencing was not performed for all patients; however, we expect that p.N409S would have been assessed for all patients. It is unknown whether patients in our study harbored other risk factors for PD such as LRRK2 variants. 28 To characterize risk of PD in a large population of patients with GD, we used data from the ICGG Gaucher Registry, which includes patients from over 60 countries and is open to any patient with GD, regardless of their treatment status or product with which they are treated. We were thus able to represent patients across a broader spectrum of the disease compared with previous studies, which is especially relevant for a disease noted for its phenotypic heterogeneity. Most of the patients in this analysis were from North America (45.3%) and Europe (52.7%) and were White (89.2%) and Ashkenazi Jewish (73.8%). This aligns with a higher observed prevalence of GD1 in these populations 29 ; however, the prevalence of GD1 in other populations, including Asia, Africa, and South America, remains incompletely understood. The generalizability of our findings to other populations, particularly those with GBA1 genotype distributions different from that of the study population, is unknown. Analysis using survival models allowed us to include nearly all patients in the Registry with data on PD and/or pPS regardless of length of follow-up, treatment status or product, or other factors, minimizing the opportunity for selection bias. Our study cohort is relatively young, with a median age of 47.8 years at last follow-up. Relatively few patients are observed at older ages; thus, associated age-specific risks (e.g., at 80 years) should be interpreted with caution. Our results will become more precise as we continue to follow this population. In this large cohort of 1,618 patients with GD1 (i.e., biallelic GBA1 pathogenic variants), we estimate that approximately 12% will develop PD by age 80 years. An even greater proportion will exhibit parkinsonian symptoms, underscoring the need for early recognition and intervention. For context, the risk of PD in the general population is approximately 1% by age 60 years and 4% by age 80 years. 30 These findings have critical implications for genetic counseling and clinical management. Genetic counselors can use these data to provide more precise risk assessments for patients with GD1, whereas clinicians should implement regular neurologic monitoring to identify early signs of PD and related movement disorders. Early referral to movement disorder specialists may facilitate timely interventions, even in the absence of disease-modifying therapies. The large proportion of patients in our study who remained free of PD, even when we used the more liberal classification of pPS, clarifies that GBA1 status does not fully explain PD penetrance. Further investigation into the factors that are protective for PD even in the setting of very low residual enzyme activity may offer valuable insights into disease pathogenesis. As GBA1 variants are among the most common genetic risk factors for PD—found in 4%–19% of PD cases 19,20 —understanding these modifiers could ultimately pave the way for targeted neuroprotective strategies, 31 benefitting both GD1 and broader PD populations.
